title: Pawn breaks: break now or prepare first?
outcomes: Chooses between playing the break and a preparatory move by counting attackers and defenders of the break square
Rejects a break when an enemy piece newly attacks the break square
Names the files a break opens and the rooks that could use them
Tells a pawn advance that attacks nothing from a real break

steps.text: In **Pawn breaks: ready or premature?** you tested whether one break was ready. Now you choose between two moves: the break itself, or a **preparatory move** that adds a defender of the break square or takes an attacker away. Count the attackers and defenders of the square the pawn lands on. Then ask what the break opens, and **who** can use the opened line first.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on d3 can step to d4 and offer an exchange against c5.

line.say: The break: the pawn attacks c5 and offers an exchange.
White recaptures. Now White has no d-pawn and Black has no c-pawn.

claims.statement: d4 is among the engine's top two moves.
After the exchange the d-file is half-open for White and the c-file is half-open for Black: the break opens a line for both sides.

steps.text: Preparation is cheap when the count is against you. *Rule of thumb:* if the break square is attacked more often than it is defended, add a defender or remove an attacker first; if the count is level or better and no pin or capture on the opened line punishes the push, break. A break opens a line for **both** sides, so look at his rooks as well as yours.

steps.title: Same break, one piece different
steps.prompt: In the first position White can play d5 now. In the second only the Black knight differs (on b6 instead of f8): break, or prepare? The third position asks a different question: does the pawn attack anything? Predict, then check.
Think of the two positions where White could play d5: the Black knight stood on f8 in one and on b6 in the other. What did you count, and which side's rooks would have used the opened files?
